chapters.title: Chapter 2: Computing a Company's Taxable Income

lessons.title: Carrying Forward Losses: How Past Losses Reduce Future Tax

body.text: A loss-making year is not wasted. The tax law lets you carry that loss into future profitable years and pay tax only on what is left. For most Indian startups, accumulated losses are the most valuable asset on the balance sheet that never appears on the balance sheet.

children.text: Businesses do not earn evenly. A manufacturer absorbs two bad years and then a strong one. A software company burns money for four years before it turns. Taxing each year in isolation would punish exactly the businesses that invest early, so the law allows losses to travel forward. It attaches conditions, though, and founders lose the benefit far more often through paperwork than through bad luck.
Set Off First, Carry Forward Later

A loss is used up in a fixed order. First it is set off against other income of the same head under section 108 [old 70], so a loss in one business reduces the profit of another business you run. Whatever remains is set off against income under other heads in the same year under section 109 [old 71]. Only what still survives is carried forward into the next year.

body.caption: Which loss goes where, and for how long

cells: Profits of any business in a later year
Income under any head except salary
Capital gains only, with long-term losses only against long-term gains
Income from house property in later years

body.text: Read the second row again. Unabsorbed depreciation never expires, and it can be set off against almost any income, not just business profit. This is why a company that has run at a loss for years while buying plant and machinery often has two very different pools of relief sitting in its file, with different rules and different shelf lives.

body.title: Two pools, two sets of rules

columns.label: Business loss under section 112 [old 72]
points: Can only be set off against business profits
Lost entirely if the return is filed late

columns.label: Unabsorbed depreciation under section 33(11) [old 32(2)]
points: Can be set off against income under any head except salary
Survives even if the return was filed late

children.text: Four Years in the Life of a Company
A Bengaluru consumer brand loses money while it builds distribution, then turns profitable. It files every return on time and is in the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA].

events.title: Loss of ₹80,00,000
events.description: No tax payable. The loss is carried forward, and the return is filed before the due date under section 263(1) [old 139(1)], which is what preserves it.

events.title: Loss of ₹40,00,000
events.description: Again no tax. Accumulated losses now stand at ₹1,20,00,000, each with its own eight-year clock running from the year it arose.

events.title: Profit of ₹30,00,000
events.description: The year 1 loss is applied first. Taxable income is nil, and ₹90,00,000 of loss remains, of which ₹50,00,000 is from year 1 and ₹40,00,000 from year 2.

events.title: Profit of ₹1,50,00,000
events.description: The remaining ₹90,00,000 is set off, leaving taxable income of ₹60,00,000 and tax of ₹15,10,080 instead of ₹37,75,200.

stats.label: Tax without carry forward

stats.label: Tax actually paid

body.title: Try It: What Is Taxable This Year?
body.prompt: A company has brought forward business losses of ₹55,00,000 from earlier years, all within the eight-year window and all supported by returns filed on time. This year it earns a business profit of ₹85,00,000. What is its taxable income? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: ₹85,00,000 less ₹55,00,000 leaves ₹30,00,000, or ₹30 lakh. At 25.168%, tax is ₹7,55,040 instead of ₹21,39,280 on the full profit. Brought forward losses are set off before unabsorbed depreciation, so if this company also had unabsorbed depreciation, that pool would only start being used once the ₹55,00,000 was exhausted.

body.title: The exact order of set-off, for the year you finally turn profitable

children.text: When a company has several kinds of relief waiting, they are applied in a set sequence. The order matters, because the pools have different expiry dates and using the wrong one first can let a good deduction lapse.

cells: Part of computing this year's business income in the first place
Brought forward business losses under section 112 [old 72]
They expire in eight years, so they are used before anything that never expires
It never expires, so it is the safest pool to leave until last

children.text: Section 112 states this directly: unabsorbed business loss is set off before any carried forward allowance under section 33(11). You do not get to choose the order, and that is deliberate, because the sequence is the one that favours the taxpayer.

body.title: Quick Check: Which One Never Expires?
body.question: A company has four kinds of relief carried forward. Which one can be used indefinitely, with no time limit?
body.explanation: Unabsorbed depreciation has no expiry and can be set off against income under any head except salary. Business and capital losses run out after eight tax years, and speculation losses after four. This is why capital-heavy businesses that lose money early often retain useful relief long after their business losses have lapsed.

children.text: Two Ways Companies Lose Their Losses

Business and capital losses can only be carried forward if the return for the loss year was filed by the due date in section 263(1) [old 139(1)]. A belated return still gets you a valid filing, but the loss does not travel. This is the single most expensive deadline a loss-making company faces, and it applies in exactly the years when nobody feels urgency about filing, because no tax is payable anyway.

body.text: Unabsorbed depreciation is the exception. It survives a late return. So a company that filed late in a loss year has not necessarily lost everything: the depreciation component of that loss may still be available. Ask your accountant to split the figure rather than assuming the whole amount is gone.

children.text: 2. Selling more than half the company

Section 119 [old 78 and 79] stops people buying loss-making companies purely for their accumulated losses. For a closely held company, brought forward losses can only be used if shareholders holding at least 51% of the voting power on the last day of the loss year still hold at least 51% on the last day of the year of set-off. Cross that line and the earlier losses are gone.

body.label: The startup exception
body.context: An eligible DPIIT-recognised startup keeps its losses through funding rounds, provided all the shareholders who held shares in the loss year continue to hold them, even if their percentage falls below 51%.

body.title: Scenario: The Round That Almost Cost ₹30 Lakh
body.scenario: A four-year-old health tech company has ₹1,20,00,000 of brought forward business losses. It is a private limited company, DPIIT-recognised, and is closing a Series A in which a fund will take 55% of the equity. One founder wants to fully exit at the same time and sell every share he holds. Separately, the finance lead mentions that the return for the second loss year was filed two months after the due date.
body.prompt: What is at risk here, and what should the company do before signing?
body.modelAnswer: Two problems, one fixable and one already done. First, the shareholding change. Ordinarily, a fund taking 55% would break the 51% continuity condition in section 119 [old 78 and 79] and wipe out the brought forward losses. The startup exception protects this company, but only if every shareholder who held shares in each loss year continues to hold shares. That is precisely what the departing founder's full exit would break. Selling most of his stake while retaining some shares would keep the exception alive, so the cap table and the exit terms should be reviewed with counsel before the round closes, not after. Second, the late return. The business loss of that year cannot be carried forward at all, because section 263(1) [old 139(1)] required it to be filed on time. The unabsorbed depreciation component of that year survives, so the company should have its accountant split the figure to see what is actually still available. The lesson for the next four years is simple: file loss year returns on the due date, even when no tax is payable, and treat every cap table change as a tax question as well as a legal one.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Clock
body.textWithBlank: A business loss under section 112 [old 72] can be carried forward for a maximum of ___ tax years after the year in which it was first computed.
body.explanation: Eight tax years, counted from the year the loss was first computed, and each year's loss runs its own clock. A loss from tax year 2026-27 is therefore available up to tax year 2034-35, after which whatever remains unused simply lapses.

body.title: Protecting Losses You Have Already Earned
steps: File the return of every loss year on or before the due date, even when there is no tax to pay
Keep a year-by-year schedule of losses showing the amount, the year it arose and the year it expires
Ask your accountant to split each loss year between business loss and unabsorbed depreciation, since they follow different rules
Check the effect on section 119 [old 78 and 79] before any funding round, buyback, founder exit or share transfer
If you are a DPIIT-recognised startup, keep that recognition current and make sure loss year shareholders retain at least some shares
Review expiring losses each year, because a loss about to lapse can change decisions on timing income or claiming deductions

body.text: Losses also matter when you buy a business. In a share purchase, the losses stay with the company and section 119 decides whether they survive the change in ownership. In an asset purchase, they stay behind with the seller. That single difference can move real money and is worth raising with your advisers early in any deal.

cards.definition: Set-off of a loss against other income under the same head in the same year.
Set-off of a remaining loss against income under other heads in the same year.
Carry forward of business losses for up to eight tax years, usable only against business profits.
Unabsorbed depreciation, carried forward indefinitely and usable against income under any head except salary.
Blocks carry forward of losses for a closely held company when 51% shareholding continuity is broken, with an exception for eligible startups.
The due date for filing the return. Miss it in a loss year and business and capital losses cannot be carried forward.
A business where contracts are settled otherwise than by actual delivery. Its losses are ring-fenced under section 113 [old 73] for four years.

points: Losses are set off within the same head under section 108 [old 70], then across heads under section 109 [old 71], and only the balance is carried forward
Business losses last eight tax years and can only be used against business profits, under section 112 [old 72]
Unabsorbed depreciation under section 33(11) [old 32(2)] never expires and can be used against almost any income
Brought forward business losses are used before unabsorbed depreciation, because they are the ones with an expiry date
Filing the loss year return by the due date in section 263(1) [old 139(1)] is what preserves the loss, and late filing destroys it

Section 119 [old 78 and 79] cancels a closely held company's losses when 51% shareholding continuity breaks, though DPIIT-recognised startups get a 10-year exception if all loss year shareholders stay on

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Rules on carry forward in mergers, demergers and business reorganisations are more detailed than the outline given here. Consult a qualified chartered accountant before relying on brought forward losses in any transaction.
